raw_response:
Catalogue-only findings for C17
Decision cutoff: 2014-04-22.

I found seven candidates. The date labels distinguish historical evidence from later or undated material; they do not assert that a live catalogue or every current feature existed at the cutoff. Application suggestions and distribution tradeoffs below are my engineering inferences, not claims that these transfers were deployed or proved useful.

1. Rust regex crate — https://github.com/rust-lang/regex
A native Rust regex library could provide succinct pattern strings, capture extraction and reusable compiled patterns behind one distribution-supported API.
Scope: general text search, runtime patterns, UTF-8 and byte-oriented inputs. Its current API illustrates compile-once reuse, including lazy initialization; that initialization still occurs at runtime. Look-around and backreferences are omitted. Date: unknown; no dated pre-cutoff version was opened.
Discovery catalogue: https://github.com/uhub/awesome-rust/blob/master/README.md
Verification: https://github.com/rust-lang/regex

2. RE2 — https://github.com/google/re2
RE2 could supply an implementation model or wrapped engine for pattern compilation, full or partial matching and capture extraction with explicit resource control.
Scope: backend and API precedent. C++ integration adds work, and its restricted dialect trades expressiveness for resource predictability. A time bound was not a mandatory input constraint. Date: pre-decision; the original implementation article is dated March 2010. Current README details are not all backdated.
Discovery catalogue: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md
Verification: https://github.com/google/re2 and https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html

3. Original PCRE — https://pcre.org/
PCRE could provide an existing C implementation and familiar Perl-style pattern language for a Rust wrapper that prioritizes broad pattern expressiveness.
Scope: native-library backend and dialect precedent. Backtracking behavior, native builds and upstream maintenance need consideration. The current site treats original PCRE as unmaintained and distinguishes PCRE2. Date: unknown for the reviewed API/version; the original changelog failed, although the 2010 RE2 article confirms PCRE already existed.
Discovery catalogue: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md
Verification: https://pcre.org/ and https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html

4. Oniguruma — https://github.com/kkos/oniguruma
Oniguruma could supply a reusable C engine and a precedent for choosing regex dialect and character-encoding behavior independently of the host language.
Scope: engine reuse and encoding policy. A Rust integration would need clear string, encoding and ownership boundaries. The current project ended in 2025. Date: pre-decision for the historical engine; HISTORY identifies 5.9.5 on 2013-10-21. This does not establish every present feature at that date.
Discovery catalogue: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md
Verification: https://github.com/kkos/oniguruma and https://github.com/kkos/oniguruma/blob/master/HISTORY

5. TRE — https://github.com/laurikari/tre
TRE could provide a POSIX-style compilation/execution interface and an optional approximate-matching mechanism when text patterns must tolerate insertions, deletions or substitutions.
Scope: interface precedent and optional fuzzy matching. Fuzzy matching expands the minimum task; backreferences and incomplete collation support require care. Date: pre-decision; its original changelog documents releases and approximate-matching changes in 2004. Current API and license details should be checked against the selected version.
Discovery catalogue: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md
Verification: https://github.com/laurikari/tre and https://github.com/laurikari/tre/blob/master/ChangeLog.old

6. Ragel — https://www.colm.net/open-source/ragel/
Ragel could inform a build-time path that compiles static text patterns into executable state machines and avoids runtime pattern parsing.
Scope: fixed-pattern generation, scanners and validation. The reviewed targets are C, C++ and assembly; Rust needs an integration layer or a generator. Build complexity, emitted-code size and embedded-action semantics remain tradeoffs. Date: later evidence; the opened page identifies 2026 releases, and no historical Ragel version was verified.
Discovery catalogue: https://aalhour.com/awesome-compilers/
Verification: https://www.colm.net/open-source/ragel/

7. CTRE — https://github.com/hanickadot/compile-time-regular-expressions
CTRE could inform a Rust static-pattern facility that validates literals during compilation and emits a specialized matcher while retaining familiar regex notation.
Scope: compile-time pattern frontend and matcher specialization. Its C++ template implementation needs translation; compilation cost and generated-code size matter. Date: later evidence; the project index dates the opened design presentation to CppCon 2018.
Discovery catalogue: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fffaraz/awesome-cpp/master/README.md
Verification: https://github.com/hanickadot/compile-time-regular-expressions and https://compile-time.re/cppcon/

Implications for a language distribution
A useful design can separate a pattern API, its execution backend and an optional static-pattern frontend. Runtime patterns remain necessary when a pattern comes from configuration or user input. Static patterns can share syntax and match-result conventions while moving validation or construction work into the build. Lazy runtime reuse is a separate implementation option and should not be described as compile-time compilation.

Bundling a supported facility reduces setup and gives users one documented default. It also commits the distribution to maintaining pattern syntax, Unicode behavior, error reporting, capture semantics and portability. Reusing C or C++ reduces how much engine code must initially be written but creates native build, ownership and upgrade work. A native Rust library can fit the host API more directly, while still imposing a long-lived maintenance burden. Providing the facility with the distribution does not by itself require new language syntax; a library API and optional compile-time frontend are separate choices.

The evidence supports comparing expressive backtracking engines with automata-based engines rather than assuming either is mandatory. Before choosing, specify which operations and syntax are actually required, whether inputs are UTF-8 or arbitrary bytes, what errors static and dynamic patterns should produce, and how much compatibility the distribution is prepared to maintain.

Search limits and omissions
Four catalogue-restricted searches produced 24 distinct page open attempts: 20 succeeded and four failed. Seven candidates were retained. CppVerbalExpressions was omitted after its primary page failed; Boost.Xpressive was not retained because no opened allowed catalogue listing established it. No target proposal was recognized or opened. This was an internal model translation exercise, not a human study; historical completeness and pretraining-memory isolation are not established.
